strengths: The paper addresses an important gap in crystal generative modeling: using one model for CSP, de novo generation, and structure-conditioned atom-type generation rather than training separate task-specific systems. The independent time axes for atom types and structures are a clean way to instantiate this any-to-any formulation.

The method is technically coherent, combining discrete flow matching for atom types, Riemannian/torus flow for fractional coordinates, and Euclidean flows for lattice parameters. The appendices provide useful algorithmic and hyperparameter detail.

Empirical coverage is fairly broad. Results on MP-20 and MPTS-52 show competitive CSP performance, especially on larger unit cells, and de novo generation results include validity, distributional fidelity, uniqueness/novelty, and CHGNet-based stability metrics.

The composition- and symmetry-aware ordering plus inter-/intra-orbit augmentation is a practical contribution. The ablations in Table 4 support its usefulness, especially for CSP match rate and MPTS-52 robustness.
Presentation is mostly clear, with well-organized method, experiments, algorithms, and metric definitions. The authors also include computational resource information and some limitations.
weaknesses: The central novelty is somewhat incremental: the multimodal flow formulation closely follows prior any-to-any multimodal flow/diffusion ideas, while the architecture is a DiT with domain-specific ordering. The paper’s contribution is useful, but not a major conceptual advance beyond adapting existing ideas to crystals.

The claim that the model learns crystallographic symmetry without templates is only partially supported. The main evidence is distributional space-group/Wyckoff statistics and ablations; there is limited direct analysis of exact symmetry satisfaction, failure modes, or how often generated structures conform to high-symmetry constraints before/after relaxation.

The atom-type generation evaluation is weak. The only baseline is CGCNN, a deterministic property-prediction-style model, and MCFlow has very low single-sample match rates despite higher compositional validity. This makes the “any-to-any” evidence less convincing for the structure-to-composition direction.

Fairness of comparisons is not always clear. Some baselines use different relaxation/evaluation settings or have missing stability metrics, and the template-conditioned comparison filters MCFlow samples by target template, which may not reflect a standard generation setting.

Reproducibility is adequate but incomplete. Hyperparameters and algorithms are listed, but the paper does not appear to commit to code/model release, and some preprocessing choices such as symmetry/orbit extraction tolerances and handling of ambiguous Wyckoff assignments are not sufficiently specified for easy replication.

The limitations discussion is brief. Scaling to larger unit cells is mentioned, but important limitations such as dependence on training-set atom-count priors, CHGNet rather than DFT validation, compute cost of 134M/464M models, and possible dataset leakage or chronological split implications are not deeply examined.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant gap: most crystal generative models are task-specific, while MCFlow attempts to support CSP, de novo generation, and structure-conditioned atom type generation with a single trained model.

The proposed combination of modality-specific flow times with a DiT backbone is conceptually clean, and the formulation is mostly understandable. The appendices provide useful algorithmic details, metric definitions, and training/inference hyperparameters.

The composition- and symmetry-aware ordering plus inter-/intra-orbit permutation augmentation is a plausible inductive bias for sequence-based transformers on crystals, and the ablation table suggests it contributes meaningfully to CSP performance, especially on MPTS-52.

The empirical evaluation covers two datasets and multiple tasks. CSP results are competitive, with particularly better MPTS-52 match rates than several non-template baselines, and MP-20 de novo generation shows strong validity and CHGNet-based stability for some model sizes.
weaknesses: The contribution is more incremental than the framing suggests. The multimodal flow idea with decoupled time axes is largely inherited from prior multimodal flow/diffusion work, and the main novelty is an application to crystals plus ordering/augmentation heuristics rather than a fundamentally new generative method.

The empirical case is not strong enough for the breadth of the claims. Many results are only competitive rather than clearly superior: MP-20 multi-sample CSP match rate is not better than CrystalFlow, DNG property distribution metrics are mixed, and S.U.N. rates are not consistently strong across model sizes.

The atom type generation task is weakly substantiated. The single-sample match rate is below the CGCNN baseline, the multi-sample setting is not directly comparable to the deterministic baseline, and the paper does not provide enough analysis to show that the generated substitutions are chemically meaningful beyond SMACT validity.

Claims that MCFlow internalizes crystallographic symmetry are overstated. The evidence is mostly distributional plots and ablations; there is no direct causal or mechanistic analysis showing that the model has learned symmetry rather than benefiting from canonical ordering and data priors.

The comparison protocol raises concerns. Template-conditioned methods are excluded from the main CSP table, then compared under a target-template-filtered setting in the appendix; this is useful but makes the main narrative somewhat selective. Several baselines also differ in training data, evaluation details, or availability of stability metrics.

Statistical rigor is limited. The paper reports point estimates without seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests, despite the use of stochastic generation, model scaling, sampling guidance, and validation-based checkpoint selection.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The appendices include many hyperparameters and algorithms, but there is no clear code release statement, exact split files/seeds, prompt/config artifacts, or sufficient detail to fully reproduce baseline comparisons and CHGNet relaxation pipelines.

The limitations and impact discussion are too shallow. The paper briefly notes scaling to larger unit cells, but does not seriously discuss failure modes, sensitivity to symmetry detection/canonicalization, dependence on empirical atom-count priors, invalid or unstable generations, or risks from automated materials generation workflows.

strengths: The paper tackles an important and well-motivated problem in crystal generative modeling: unifying CSP, de novo generation, and structure-conditioned atom-type generation in a single model rather than training task-specific systems. The independent time axes for atom types and structures are a clean way to instantiate any-to-any conditional generation in this domain.

The proposed composition- and symmetry-aware atom ordering, together with inter- and intra-orbit permutation augmentation, is a practical and domain-informed contribution. It gives a standard DiT backbone useful crystallographic and compositional priors without requiring explicit structural templates at inference time.

The empirical evaluation is broad and relevant. Results cover MP-20 and MPTS-52, three model scales, CSP, DNG, and atom-type generation, with comparisons to many recent baselines. The MPTS-52 results are especially useful because they test robustness on larger unit cells.

The ablations support the main design choices: removing inter-orbit augmentation, intra-orbit augmentation, and positional/order information consistently hurts CSP and/or compositional validity, with larger drops on MPTS-52. The noisy-guidance and integration-step analyses add useful evidence about inference behavior.

Reproducibility is reasonably supported by detailed architecture, training, inference, metric, and compute descriptions in the appendix. The paper also reports practical details such as integration steps, model sizes, loss weights, checkpoint selection, and CHGNet-based stability evaluation.
weaknesses: The novelty is meaningful but somewhat incremental at the framework level: decoupled modality-wise flow times are adapted from prior multimodal flow/diffusion work, and the main originality lies in the crystal-specific instantiation and ordering/augmentation strategy. The paper could more sharply separate what is new from what is inherited from Multiflow and related multimodal diffusion frameworks.

Some claims about learning crystallographic symmetry without explicit constraints are stronger than the evidence warrants. The model uses Wyckoff positions during preprocessing/order construction, so crystallographic information is not fully absent; it is encoded as a training-time inductive bias rather than enforced at generation time. This distinction should be stated more carefully.

The baseline comparison is generally strong, but not always perfectly clean. MCFlow-L is much larger than several baselines, and different baselines use different conditioning assumptions, templates, relaxation/evaluation protocols, or external modules. The paper discusses template-conditioned methods separately, which helps, but the main tables still require careful interpretation.

The atom-type generation task is less convincingly evaluated than CSP and DNG. The only quantitative baseline is CGCNN, which is deterministic and not a strong generative comparator; the low match rates also make it unclear how useful this task is beyond demonstrating the any-to-any capability.

The limitations and ethics discussion are light. The paper notes scaling to larger unit cells as a challenge, but says little about failure modes, sensitivity to symmetry detection/preprocessing, invalid high-confidence samples, dataset bias from Materials Project, or downstream risks of suggesting unstable or impractical materials.

No code release is indicated in the manuscript. Although the appendix gives many implementation details, full reproducibility would benefit from released preprocessing scripts, ordering/augmentation code, exact dataset splits, and evaluation pipelines, especially because symmetry preprocessing and StructureMatcher/CHGNet choices can materially affect results.

strengths: The paper presents a coherent unified formulation for crystal generation, using separate flow time axes for atom types and structures to realize CSP, de novo generation, atom-type generation, and masked substitution with one trained model. This is a useful contribution in a literature dominated by task-specific models.

The method is technically plausible and reasonably well specified: the manuscript defines the multimodal path, continuous/discrete flow objectives, torus treatment for fractional coordinates, DiT parameterization, noisy guidance, and inference algorithms.

The empirical coverage is broad. Results are reported on MP-20 and MPTS-52 across CSP, DNG, ATG, ablations, model scales, compute cost, polymorph-aware metrics, and template-conditioned comparisons. The MPTS-52 CSP improvements and the decoupled-time ablation are particularly supportive of the central design.

The composition- and symmetry-aware ordering plus hierarchical permutation augmentation is a practical inductive bias for applying sequence Transformers to crystals, and the ablations suggest it materially improves CSP and DNG validity.

Reproducibility is stronger than average for an experimental ML paper: architecture sizes, training hyperparameters, inference settings, metrics, tolerances, and algorithms are given in appendices, and limitations/impact are discussed without obvious ethical concerns.
weaknesses: The originality is moderate rather than exceptional. The decoupled time-axis multimodal flow idea is adapted from recent multimodal flow/diffusion work; the main novelty is its crystal-specific instantiation and ordering/augmentation scheme rather than a fundamentally new generative principle.

Some central claims are overstated. In de novo generation, MCFlow improves stability-related metrics but has much lower novelty than several baselines, especially for the larger models. SUN/MSUN results are mixed, so the claim of broadly superior DNG performance should be framed more cautiously.

The DNG comparison is hard to interpret because models are split into pre-relaxed and non-pre-relaxed groups, and MCFlow uses Orb-v3 for pre-relaxation while evaluation also uses an MLIP ensemble including Orb-v3. This may advantage MCFlow on stability metrics and weakens conclusions about unconditional sample quality.

The atom type generation task is interesting but not yet very convincing: single-sample match rates are very low, the baseline set is limited/adapted, and the qualitative substitution examples are too small to establish a robust new capability.

The symmetry-aware ordering uses Wyckoff/orbit information during preprocessing, but for CSP the structure and Wyckoff labels are unavailable at inference. The paper would benefit from a clearer explanation of how this train-time structural ordering transfers to composition-only inference and whether it introduces train/inference mismatch.

Evaluation uncertainty is underreported. Standard deviations are mainly across generated structures or MLIPs rather than across training seeds/runs, and many comparisons involve large models and different sampling/pre-relaxation budgets. Statistical robustness of the reported margins is therefore unclear.

No code or trained-model release is mentioned. Although the hyperparameter details are extensive, reproducing the full pipeline likely requires substantial crystallographic preprocessing, MLIP relaxation, and benchmark integration effort.

strengths: The paper addresses a real limitation of current crystal generative models: most are task-specific, whereas MCFlow uses separate time axes for atom types and structures to support CSP, de novo generation, and structure-conditioned atom-type generation in one model.

The experimental section is broad. It evaluates on MP-20 and MPTS-52, includes multiple model scales, compares against several recent baselines, and reports ablations for ordering, inter/intra-orbit permutation, noisy guidance, and coupled versus decoupled time axes.

Some empirical results are promising: MCFlow is competitive on CSP, especially on MPTS-52; the ordering and permutation ablations show nontrivial gains; and the de novo validity/stability metrics improve over several baselines under the chosen LeMat-GenBench protocol.
The paper is generally readable, with a clear high-level formulation and useful appendices describing flow targets, model/training settings, metrics, and computational cost.

The limitations section honestly notes two important constraints: dependence on well-defined crystallographic symmetry, which excludes amorphous/disordered systems, and a stability-novelty tradeoff across model scales.
weaknesses: The central originality is limited. The multimodal decoupled-time formulation is largely an application of existing multimodal flow/diffusion ideas to crystals, and the DiT backbone plus clean-data prediction are also standard choices. The main domain-specific contribution is the atom ordering/augmentation scheme, which is useful but not enough to make the work feel conceptually strong for ICML.

The empirical case does not consistently support the paper's stronger claims. On MP-20 CSP, MCFlow-L single-sample MR is only slightly above OMatG and comparable to other baselines; with 20 samples, MCFlow has lower MR than DiffCSP/CrystalFlow on MP-20 despite better RMSE. Thus the method is not clearly state of the art on a core benchmark.

The de novo generation results are hard to interpret because the strongest headline stability numbers rely on MLIP pre-relaxation, while novelty drops severely with model scale: MCFlow-B/L with pre-relaxation report only 25.4/18.6 percent novelty, and SUN remains tiny. This weakens the claim that the model discovers broadly useful new materials rather than generating stable-looking variants near known regions.

The atom-type generation task is underdeveloped as evidence for any-to-any modeling. Single-sample match rates are extremely low, sometimes below the CGCNN reference, and even 20-sample MR remains modest. The baselines are adapted rather than established for this task, so the evaluation does not convincingly demonstrate a practically useful new capability.

Several comparisons raise fairness concerns. Template-conditioned methods are excluded from the main CSP table as a different setting, but later compared under target-template filtering; DNG baselines are split into pre-relaxed and non-pre-relaxed groups; and MCFlow uses noisy guidance for single-sample conditional tasks. The paper does not fully disentangle architectural benefits, guidance, scale, pre-relaxation, and evaluation protocol choices.

The proposed ordering depends on extracting space-group/Wyckoff information from the target training structures. While the paper says it avoids explicit templates at inference, the method still uses crystallographic analysis as preprocessing and does not sufficiently analyze robustness to symmetry detection tolerances, noisy/relaxed structures, or ambiguous Wyckoff assignments.

Ablations are useful but incomplete. There is no clean comparison to a DiT with simpler composition ordering and equal parameter/training budget across all tasks, and the positional embedding ablation is an indirect test of ordering rather than a full isolation of the claimed symmetry prior. The evidence that the model 'internalizes crystallographic symmetry' relies mostly on aggregate distributions rather than stricter structural validation.

Reproducibility is only partial. Hyperparameters, model sizes, and metrics are documented, but the manuscript does not appear to provide code, trained checkpoints, random seeds, exact data split identifiers, or detailed baseline reproduction settings. Given the complexity of LeMat-GenBench, MLIP ensembles, pre-relaxation, and symmetry analysis, this is a material weakness.

The impact statement is generic and does not meaningfully discuss risks or limitations around ML-generated materials, potential false positives from learned potentials, computational/energy costs of large models, or downstream validation requirements. There are no obvious severe ethical concerns, but the treatment is shallow.

Overall, the paper has useful engineering and some solid experimental work, but the contribution feels incremental, the main claims are stronger than the evidence, and the evaluation leaves too many interpretation gaps for acceptance in the main track without substantial revision.

strengths: The paper presents a coherent and useful unification of several crystal generation tasks. Decoupling atom-type and structure flow time axes is a natural but effective way to realize CSP, de novo generation, and structure-conditioned atom-type generation in one model without retraining.

The empirical evaluation is broad and mostly convincing: results cover MP-20 and MPTS-52, single- and multi-sample CSP, de novo generation under LeMat-GenBench, atom-type generation, scaling behavior, computational cost, noisy-guidance sensitivity, polymorph-aware evaluation, and several targeted ablations.

The proposed composition- and symmetry-aware ordering plus hierarchical permutation augmentation is well motivated for adapting a DiT backbone to crystals. The ablations in Tables 5 and H.4 show meaningful drops when removing inter-orbit permutation, intra-orbit permutation, positional embeddings, or the electronegativity ordering.

The results are significant for the area: MCFlow is competitive or stronger than task-specific baselines on CSP, especially on MPTS-52, and obtains strong validity and stability metrics for de novo generation while avoiding explicit symmetry-template conditioning.

Presentation is generally clear. The paper gives mathematical details, algorithms, training/inference configurations, metric definitions, and computational resources, which makes the method relatively easy to understand and partially reproducible.

The limitations section is honest about the reliance on well-defined crystallographic symmetry and the stability-novelty trade-off. I do not see major unresolved ethical concerns; the impact statement is appropriate for computational materials discovery.
weaknesses: The main methodological novelty is somewhat incremental relative to prior multimodal flow work such as Multiflow/Diffuse Everything; the contribution is primarily the adaptation and engineering of this paradigm to crystal generation, plus the ordering/augmentation scheme, rather than a fundamentally new generative principle.

Reproducibility is incomplete without an explicit code/model/data release statement. The appendix gives many hyperparameters and resource details, but exact preprocessing details for symmetry/orbit extraction, checkpoint selection, baseline reproduction, and inference scripts would be needed for others to reliably reproduce the numbers.

The de novo generation comparisons are somewhat hard to interpret because the table mixes models with and without MLIP pre-relaxation, and MCFlow uses Orb-v3 pre-relaxation in the relaxed setting. Strong stability metrics after relaxation are useful, but they partially reflect the relaxation pipeline rather than only the generator.

The atom-type generation task is interesting but less established, and the baselines are relatively weak or adapted from other settings. The very low one-sample match rates make it hard to assess how much this task demonstrates practical structure-to-composition discovery beyond compositional validity.

Some claims around learning crystallographic symmetry without explicit templates should be stated carefully: the method does use space-group/Wyckoff information during preprocessing for ordering and augmentation, even if it does not condition on templates at inference time.

The method is limited to ordered crystalline systems with identifiable symmetry. This is acknowledged, but it narrows the scope and means the approach may not transfer directly to disordered, defective, amorphous, surface, or finite-material settings.
